scenes.narration: Input gives text, and maths needs numbers. Today we learn how to change one type into another, and what happens when it goes wrong.

scenes.onScreen: "Changing types": three numbered lines (1. int() makes a whole number; 2. float() makes a decimal; 3. str() makes text) and an analogy card: a currency counter: the same value, written in a different note
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Python has three conversion tools. The int function makes a whole number. The float function makes a decimal. The str function makes text. Think of a currency counter. The value is the same, but it is written on a different note. The conversion makes a new object. The old one is left as it was. If the text cannot be a number, Python raises an error.

code.source:
text = "42"
number = int(text)
print(number + 8)
print(float("3.5") * 2)
print(str(7) + " beaches")

scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name text is still tied to the string forty two. The name number is tied to a brand new int, forty two. They look alike when printed, but they are different objects of different types. A string can join, and an int can add. Conversion is how you move between the two.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: int of a word
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We ask int to turn the word abc into a number. Python says, value error, invalid literal for int. The text must look like a whole number. Digits are fine. Letters are not. The last line tells you the exact text that failed, which makes the bug easy to find. Fix the text, and it works.

shorts.title: Three conversion tools
shorts.script: Python has three conversion tools. The int function makes a whole number. The float function makes a decimal. The str function makes text. Each one gives you a brand new object, and leaves the old one as it was. So int of the string forty two gives the number forty two. Learn these three, and you can move between types easily. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Change the type.

shorts.title: Read a number
shorts.hook: "Here is the pattern every program uses to read a number."
shorts.script: Here is the pattern every program uses to read a number. Age equals int, open bracket, input, open bracket, the question, close bracket, close bracket. Input asks and gives text. Int turns the text into a number. Then you can add, compare and multiply as much as you like. Read it from the inside out, and it makes sense. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: The read-a-number pattern.

shorts.title: A new object
shorts.hook: "When you convert, Python makes a new object."
shorts.script: When you convert, Python makes a new object. The name text still points at the string forty two. The name number points at a new int, forty two. They print the same, but they behave differently. A string can join with another string. An int can do maths. Pick the type that does the job you need. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Conversion makes a new value.

shorts.title: Value error
shorts.hook: "What if the text is not a number?"
shorts.script: What if the text is not a number? Int of the word abc does not work. Python says value error, invalid literal for int. The text must look like a whole number, so digits are fine, and letters are not. The last line shows the exact text that failed. Check what your user typed, and the bug becomes easy to see. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Letters are not digits.

shorts.hook: "Why did the string go to therapy?"
shorts.script: Why did the string go to therapy? It had trouble converting its feelings into numbers. Your challenge. Ask the user for a number. Then print double that number. Remember, input gives text, so convert it with int first. If the user types twenty one, your program should print forty two. Share your code in the comments, please. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
